newsitem.title: USA: Northeast states critical of Midwest coal plants.
newsitem.headline: Northeast states critical of Midwest coal plants.

text.p: Northeastern governors agreed Friday to push for tighter regulations on polluting Midwestern power plants, but distanced themselves from calls for a regional boycott of the electricity they produce.

The governors said forcing those coal-powered plants to meet stricter emmissions standards was needed to ease the Northeast's pollution problems and allow its utilities to compete in a deregulated market for electricity.
"The point is if we're serious about the idea (of reducing pollution) then it has to be a national effort," Maine Gov. Angus King told Reuters at meeting of the Coalition of Northeastern Governors.
The coalition agreed to explore ways to end the exemption from the Federal Clean Act given about 700 coal-fired power plants when the law was enacted in 1997.
The group, which includes Maine, New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Connecticut, Massachusetts, New Hampshire and Vermont, hopes to have a formal proposal for its February meeting.
Some of the older "grandfathered" power plants are located in the northeast, but most are located in the Ohio river valley and other regions of the Midwest - upwind of the northeastern states.

The governors complained Friday that with the EPA proposing new stricter air quality standards, it will be impossible for many of their states to comply unless pollution that comes into the region is also reduced.
Midwestern utility officials and politicians have scoffed at the Northeast's complaints, charging that there is no scientific data to support the claim and it is only an attempt to shift blame.

The Northeastern governors also said bringing the older generating facilities into compliance would also "level the playing field" for utilities with newer facilities that cost more to operate because of pollution controls.

Environmental officials worry that because many of the coal fired plants are cheaper to operate, the pollution problem will increase as the electric industry is deregulated and power plants compete against each other.

Vermont Gov. Howard Dean, the coalition's outgoing president, said he was interested in having the region use its market power in purchasing electricity to force utilities to meet tougher environmental standards.
"We have not been able to succeede through regulations, perhaps we can succeede through the market place," Dean told reporters.

Massachusetts Attorney General Scott Harshbarger has proposed the 12 east and northeastern states, from Virginia to Maine, form a regional compact that might impose surcharges on "dirty" power or boycott electricity from polluting plants.

The governors distanced themselves from the boycott idea, questioning both its legality and effectiveness - because the Midwestern electricity could still be sold to other regions of the United States.
"The problem I have with a boycott is that we could end up with the worst of both worlds," said King. "The Southwest will get cheap electricity ... and we will get the pollution."
